activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Chloe went to the store with Dad. She wanted a red apple. Outside the store, they had to cross the road. Dad held her hand tight.

"Look, Dad, a light!" said Chloe. It was up high on a pole. The light turned red. All the cars stopped. Then the light turned green. All the cars started to go. "Red means stop. Green means go!" said Chloe. Dad laughed. "Yes, let's go now." The light was green, so they walked.

Inside the store, Chloe saw yellow bananas and green grapes. She picked one big red apple. It felt heavy in her hands. On the way out, a little boy was crying by the toy pig. Chloe gave him a wave. He smiled at her. At the crossing, the light turned red again. "Stop!" said Chloe. Dad squeezed her hand. The cars stopped, and they waited for green.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Nathan went to the park with his dad. They were bringing home a new pet. It was a small guinea pig named Pip. Nathan wanted to carry Pip all around.

"I can hold him while I run," said Nathan.

Dad shook his head. "Let us sit on the grass first," he said. They sat down. Dad showed Nathan how to use two hands. "Hold him gently," said Dad. "Not too tight."

Nathan held Pip with two hands. Pip was soft and warm. Pip wiggled a little. Nathan sat very still. Pip did not fall at all.

Then a baby bird hopped near them. Pip made a happy squeak. What a small surprise!

"Again!" said Nathan. He held Pip gently, gently, with two hands. Then they walked home, slow and happy, Pip squeaking all the way.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Charles was at school. Today was a big day. He was going to write his own name!

Ms. Amy gave him a chunky pencil. She gave him a paper with the letters C-H-A-R-L-E-S.

Charles picked up the pencil. He began to trace the C. But the paper slid away! His line went crooked. "Oh no," said Charles.

He tried again. He took off his shoe and tried to hold the paper with his foot. That did not work at all. The paper still slipped. Everyone giggled.

Then Charles had an idea. He put his shoe back on. He pressed his other hand flat on the paper. The paper stopped sliding!

He traced the C. It came out round and neat. He traced the H. Then the A. His letters went up and up, all the way to the S.

"I did it!" said Charles. Ms. Amy put his paper on the wall. Charles stood in his cozy sweater and clapped his hands.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Elijah went to the vet with his mom. A small puppy sat in a crate. "Can he be my pet?" Elijah asked. "Yes," said Mom. "He is ours now."

The vet clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. The leash went from the collar to Mom's hand. "I will walk him," said Mom. Outside, a bird hopped on the grass. The puppy wanted to chase it. He pulled and pulled. But the leash kept him close to Mom. He could not run away. "The leash holds him!" said Elijah. "Is that what it does?" "Yes," said Mom. "It keeps him near us."

At home, the puppy's tummy made a big growl. Was he grumpy? No, he was hungry. Mom poured food in his bowl. The puppy ate it all up. Then he curled up on Elijah's lap. "I will walk you every day," Elijah whispered. The puppy licked his hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Rosalie ran up the steps to Grandma's house. The door opened fast. "Happy Hanukkah!" said Grandma. Inside, the house smelled like warm potato pancakes. Cousin Ben was already at the table. Rosalie had not seen Ben for a long, long time.

"Ben!" she called. "You got so big!" Ben laughed and showed her his new truck. It had a black wheel that spun around. Rosalie spun it too. It went whir, whir, whir.

Then Daddy came in with the menorah. He lit the candles with a match. Rosalie stood back and watched the little flames. "One, two, three candles," she counted. The candles made the room glow. "Why so many candles tonight?" she wondered. Grandma smiled and patted the big chair. "Everyone sit close," she said. "The family is all here now."

Ben handed Rosalie a small gift. It was a dreidel with short sides. "Spin it," said Ben. Rosalie spun it on the table. Round and round it went, and then it fell with a tap. "My turn," said Ben. He spun it back to her.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Austin went to the store with Mom. He wanted one big orange carrot. He was a bunny today, and bunnies need carrots.

The carrot aisle was busy. A tall man stood in the way. Austin squeezed and squeezed. He could not get past. "Mom, I'm stuck," he said.

"Try the magic words," Mom said. Austin thought hard. Then he looked up at the man. "Excuse me, please," he said. The man smiled and stepped aside. "Thank you!" said Austin. He zoomed past like a little bunny.

Austin found the biggest carrot of all. It looked like a magic wand. He put it in the cart, next to the frozen peas. At the checkout, he bumped the cart into a shelf. A can fell down. "Sorry," said Austin. He picked up the can and put it back.

At home, Mom washed the carrot. Austin held it up high. "Abracadabra!" he said. "Now we are bunny wizards." Mom laughed and took a big crunchy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp glowed warm and yellow. Her plate had peas, bread, and milk.

"Papa, story now," said Sophia.

"A story is not now," said Papa. "Now we eat dinner. The story comes later, after dinner."

Sophia looked at her plate. She ate one pea. Then she ate two peas. "One pea, two peas, three peas," she counted. The peas went into her tummy, one by one.

She took a big drink of milk. Oops. The cup tipped. Milk ran across the table. "Messy," said Sophia.

Papa brought a towel. He helped her wipe the table. "The milk spilled now," said Papa. "Now we clean it up." They wiped and wiped until the table was dry again.

Sophia shook her napkin open. She put it on her lap, all by herself. She ate her bread. She ate more peas. Her plate was empty at last.

"Dinner is done," said Papa. "Now it is story time."

Sophia clapped her hands. "Now? Now the story?"

"Yes, now," said Papa. He sat down next to her. He opened the big story book.

Sophia snuggled close. "Yesterday we read the bear book," she said.

"That's right," said Papa. "Today we read this one. Tomorrow we can pick a new book."

Sophia smiled. "Today is story day." Papa turned the first page, and he began, "Once there was a little duck."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Olivia wanted to paint a big sky. She had red, yellow and blue paint. She knew their names now. "Red like a strawberry," she said. "Yellow like the sun. Blue like my cup."

She set up her wooden easel. She dipped her brush in the blue. She painted a big blue sky. Then she stepped back to look. "Oh no," she said. "My sky is too dark. It looks like night!"

She wanted a morning sky. A light blue sky. She looked at her paints. Then she had a question. "What if I add white?"

She found the white paint. She stirred it into the blue. Round and round went the brush. The blue began to change. It got lighter and lighter. "Look, look!" she shouted. "My sky is getting soft!"

She painted the light blue over the dark blue. Now it looked like morning. Dad came to see. "Did you paint that?" he asked. Olivia grinned. "I did! White made my blue light!" Then she dipped her brush again. "Now I will paint a yellow sun."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Mya sat on the playroom rug. She had five toy monkeys. She wanted to sing their song. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," she sang. "One fell off and bumped his head!" She made one monkey fall down. It rolled under the chair. She counted the monkeys left on the rug. "One, two, three, four," she said.

She sang the next part. "Mama called the doctor and the doctor said..." She made her voice deep like Daddy's. "No more monkeys jumping on the bed!" Then she sang again. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" Another monkey fell. This one landed on her foot. She giggled and put it with the first monkey. "One, two, three," she counted.

Mya went on singing. Each time the song said a monkey fell, she took one away. Three monkeys, then two, then one. The last monkey had a big job. It jumped all alone. "One little monkey jumping on the bed!" Mya sang loud. Then it fell too, right into her lap.

Mya looked at her empty rug. All the monkeys were in her lap now. "Zero monkeys," she said. Her little brother crawled over. He wanted a monkey too. "You are lucky," Mya said. "I have five!" She handed him one. Then she counted what she had left. "One, two, three, four." She hugged the monkeys and started the song again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Blake's teddy bear, Boo, was sick. He had a big cough. "Ah-choo!" said Blake for him. She put Boo in a small box. The box was his bed. "You need medicine," Blake told him.

She ran to the kitchen. Mom was there. "Can I have pretend medicine?" Blake asked. Mom gave her a spoon of water. "Only pretend," said Mom. Blake held the spoon near Boo's mouth. Boo drank it all up. Then Blake wrapped Boo in her old blue blanket. She tucked him in. She gave him a kiss on his nose.

Boo opened one eye. He felt better already! Blake said, "Your job is to sleep now." She turned off the light. From the dark came a tiny sound. "Ah-choo!" Blake ran back. "Boo! You need a hat too."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Jacob ran to the playground. The big slide waited for him. The small slide waited too. "Which one should I ride?" he asked. "The big one!" said his friend Mia.

The sun was hot. The water fountain was cold. Jacob drank and drank.

Then it was quiet time. Baby Ben was sleeping on a blanket. Jacob wanted to bang his drum. Boom! Boom! So loud! Mama put her finger to her lips. "Shh. The drum woke the baby."

"Can a drum be quiet?" Jacob asked himself. He tried a little tap. Tap. Tap. So quiet! Baby Ben kept sleeping.

After nap, Jacob tapped fast. Then he tapped slow. Ben laughed and clapped.

"Your drum is a good gift," said Mia. She sniffed her shoe. "My sock is smelly!" Everybody laughed. Jacob tapped one more quiet tap. "Shh," he whispered, grinning.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Jake was at school. He wanted to play outside on the slide. Then the sky got dark. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"No park," said his teacher, Miss Kim. Jake felt sad. His lip went down. He sat on the rug and looked at the wet window.

Then Mia came over. "Let's make a blanket house," she said. They put a big blanket on two chairs. It made a soft little cave. Jake crawled inside. It smelled clean, like fresh towels. He smiled a big smile.

"I feel happy now," said Jake. Miss Kim laughed softly. "The rain gave us a surprise," she said.

Jake heard the rain tap again. It sounded like a song. "Rain, rain, spell your name," sang Mia. Jake sang too, inside their cozy blanket house.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Edouard saw a big blue truck at the park. It was full of books. A man inside gave books to kids. Edouard wanted a book too. But the man said, "You need a card."

Edouard patted his pockets. He had no card. He ran to his grandma. "Can you help me get one?" he begged. Grandma smiled and took his hand. They went to the little desk in the truck. The man gave them a paper to write on. Grandma wrote her name. Then Edouard wrote his name, all wobbly. The man gave Edouard a small blue card. "This card is yours," he said.

Edouard picked a book about a sleepy bear. The bear fell asleep in a cave. Edouard held the book tight all the way home. At bedtime he read it two times. Then he put the card under his pillow.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Sara ran to the park with her bunny. She squeezed him tight. But at the swings, her hands let go. Bunny was gone!

Sara looked and looked. One swing, two swings, no bunny. One slide, two slides, no bunny. A dog barked near the bench. No bunny there either.

Then Sara saw a little house. It had a sign with a hat and a shoe on it. A kind man opened the door. Inside were lost things. A thin scarf hung on a hook. A red cup sat on a shelf. One box, two boxes, three boxes of hats!

"Things people find go in here," the man said. "Look inside this basket." Sara peeked in. Soft gray ears popped up at her. Bunny!

Sara hugged him all the way home. "One swing, two swings," she sang, "and one bunny, found!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Mia wanted cold milk. She was so thirsty after helping Papa shop for big oranges and small plums. "One bag, two bags, three bags," she had counted at the store.

She opened the fridge door. The milk was cold inside. Then Mama called, "Mia, come see the tea!" Mia ran fast to the table. Mama poured hot tea from the pot. "Blow on it," said Mama. "It is hot. Your milk is cold."

Mia blew. The steam went up, up, up. Then she heard a humming sound. She looked back at the fridge. The door was open! Cold air was puffing out. Mia walked slow and careful. She pushed the door shut. The humming stopped. "All closed," said Mia. "Now the milk stays cold, and I can drink it." She took a big sip.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Scarlett sat on the red rug at school. Miss Ana held up a big blue bag. "Let's play the feely-bag game," she said. "Put your hand in. Don't peek. Guess the toy!"

Tom went first. He put his hand in the bag. "It is a ball," he said. He pulled it out. The ball was yellow. "I thought it was red," said Tom. "The bag tricked me!"

Now it was Scarlett's turn. She closed her eyes and pushed her hand in. She felt something round and smooth. She squeezed it. She pat pat patted it. "Is it a ball?" she asked. "Yes!" said Miss Ana. "But what color is it?" Scarlett felt and felt. "I can't tell," she said. "My fingers can't see." She pulled out the ball. It was green, her favorite color! Everyone clapped.

Scarlett had an idea. "Let me try one more," she said. She felt inside the bag. Something small and bumpy. "A car!" she said. "But I must look for the color." Out came a blue car. "Blue!" she shouted. Tom laughed. "The game is tricky," he said. "My fingers know the shape. Only my eyes know the color."

At play time, Scarlett made a sign for the bag. She drew a big eye on it. Tom drew a hand next to it. "Eye for colors," said Scarlett. "Hand for shapes." They hung the sign on the wall. "Next time, I will guess better," said Tom. Scarlett smiled and patted the green ball. "Me too," she said. "But green is still my favorite."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Zoe rode in the car with Daddy. They drove down the long road to the hospital. The sky was cloudy and gray. Mommy was at the hospital with a new baby.

Zoe held Daddy's hand in the hall. They found Mommy's room. Mommy was in the big bed. Next to her was a small basket. Inside was a tiny baby. "This is your brother," Mommy said.

The baby began to cry. The nurse said, "He needs a clean diaper." Daddy looked in the bag. He could not find one. Zoe saw something under the blanket. "I will look," she said. She lifted the soft blanket. A clean diaper was hiding there. She gave it to the nurse.

The nurse changed the baby. He stopped crying. He looked at Zoe. Mommy smiled. "You helped him," she said.

Zoe patted the baby's small hand. The baby held her finger. Daddy brought a warm blanket. Zoe helped tuck it in around him. "Hello, baby brother," Zoe whispered. "I will help you every day."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Elena sat on her soft rug. The sun made a warm spot by her bed. Her toy bunny, Boo, sat in a little boat made of a shoebox. The boat was a boat on a pretend pond.

Elena pushed the boat gently. Then she pushed too hard. The boat tipped over. Boo fell out and bumped the floor. Elena felt scared. She held her breath.

She picked Boo up and looked at his face. "Are you okay?" she asked. Boo stayed quiet. Elena hugged him soft and close. She patted his ears. Then she felt happy again. Her tummy felt warm.

Elena set Boo back in the boat. "I will send you across the pond," she said. She blew a little puff of air. It was like a windy day for Boo. The boat moved slow across the rug. Boo did not fall this time. Elena clapped her hands. "You did it!" she said. She gave Boo one more gentle push and watched him float.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Mason sat at Grandma's big table. He held a fat yellow pencil. "I want to write my name," he said. "Can I?" Grandma smiled. "Yes. Let me show you how to hold it." She put his fingers on the pencil. Three fingers, just like that.

Mason made an M. It looked wobbly, like a cat had walked across the paper. He laughed. "Silly M!" He tried again. Still wobbly. "Why is it so hard?" he asked. Grandma said, "Try it lots of times." So Mason wrote M, M, M. Then A, S, O, N. He was not afraid of the wiggly letters anymore.

Every day at Grandma's house, Mason wrote his name. One, two, three letters, then four, then five. Soon the M stood up straight. The O turned into a nice round circle. "Look, Grandma!" said Mason. Grandma clapped. "That says Mason!" Mason held up his paper high and said, "That's me!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Owen came to the playground early. The sun felt warm on his face. He heard kids laughing on the swings.

Owen ran to the slide. But a big boy was there. The big boy pushed in front of Owen. Owen felt angry. His face got hot. He wanted to stomp his feet. He sat on a bench instead. The bench felt cool and smooth.

His teacher Miss Ana sat down next to him. "Owen, how are you feeling?" she asked. Owen looked at his shoes. "I feel sad," he said. "I feel angry too. That boy pushed ahead of me." Miss Ana nodded. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Let's go talk to him together." The big boy said sorry. Then he slid down and clapped for Owen's turn.

Owen slid down fast. The wind whooshed by his ears. He felt excited and happy. He ran to tell Miss Ana. "My tummy tickled!" he said. She smiled and held his hand. It was soft like his pillow at home. They walked to the swings, nice and slow. Owen pumped his legs higher and higher. "I feel so happy!" he shouted. Miss Ana clapped and said, "I can tell!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Matteo ran to the pool in his thick swim shorts. He was ready to jump in. "Stop right there," a lifeguard called out. "Shower first, then swim."

Matteo looked at the pool. The water looked big and shiny. He looked at the shower. The water there was small and warm. Matteo did not want the small water. He wanted the big water.

"Shower first, then swim," Mom said with a smile. Matteo stood under the shower. The warm water ran over his hair. It ran over his arms. "Shower first, then swim," Matteo said this time, all by himself.

Then he walked to the pool steps. Splash! His feet went in. The water was cool. "I showered first!" Matteo shouted. Then something surprising happened. Another boy ran past him, straight toward the pool. The lifeguard said the same words. "Shower first, then swim."

The boy stopped. He looked at Matteo. Matteo pointed at the shower. "Warm water," he said. "It is nice." The boy stood under it too.

Then the two boys sat on the pool step together. Splash went Matteo's hands. Splash went the boy's hands. "Shower first, then swim," they both said, and in they went.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Layla woke up with funny hair. It stood up on one side. It flopped over the other side.

She hopped out of bed. She looked in the little mirror. "My hair looks like a bird nest!" she said. Her socks peeked out of the covers like two sleepy mice. Layla laughed and put them on her feet.

"I want to look nice today," Layla said. Mommy was awake too. "Ask me for the brush," said Mommy. Layla asked. Mommy gave her the soft blue brush.

Layla brushed the top. That part was easy. Then she came to a tangle. Ouch! It pulled. "Go slow," said Mommy. "Little bits at a time." Layla brushed one little bit. Then another little bit. The tangle got smaller and smaller. Then it was gone! Layla smiled big. Her hair was smooth and shiny.

After that, Layla had a bath with bubbles. She got dressed all by herself. She ate eggs for breakfast. Her heart felt happy and bouncy. She ran to show Daddy her hair.

"Look at my smooth hair!" said Layla. Daddy patted it gently. "Very nice," he said. "Can I borrow your brush? My hair looks like a bird nest too!"

Layla giggled and handed him the blue brush.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Evan ran to the sandbox. He wanted the big yellow digger. It was his turn now. Ben had it last.

But the door was open. The little babies were sleeping inside on soft mats. Evan did not know yet.

"I WANT THE DIGGER!" Evan shouted very loud. A baby inside woke up and began to cry. Miss Amy came out fast. She put her finger by her lips. "The babies are sleeping," she said in a small, small voice. "Come with me."

Evan stood still. He heard the baby cry. Then the baby stopped. Miss Amy rocked her gently. Evan watched. When someone sleeps, you need a quiet voice, he thought. Would a whisper work?

Evan leaned close to Ben. "Can I have the digger next?" he whispered. Ben nodded. He dug one more scoop of sand. Then he gave Evan the digger.

Evan dug a big hole. He put a stick in the hole like a tree. "Look at my tree," he whispered. The babies kept sleeping. Miss Amy smiled and gave them both a cracker.

"Quiet voices all morning?" Evan whispered to Ben. Ben held his cracker up high. "Yes," he whispered back.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Wyatt ran to the slide at school. The ladder went up, up, up. Wyatt climbed to the top. Then he slid down, down, down. "Again!" he said. He went up and down many times.

His friend Milo was little. Milo's legs felt weak at the bottom of the ladder. He could not climb up. Wyatt saw Milo's sad face. He held Milo's hand. "One step," said Wyatt. "Then one more." Up they went, slow and slow. Then they slid down, fast and fast. Milo laughed out loud.

After the slide, they went inside. Miss Jo had a big cup of tea. The tea was hot. She held it with both hands. "Careful," she said. She gave the boys small cups of cold water. Wyatt drank his cold water fast. Milo drank his slow. Then Wyatt and Milo sat at the table. They used blocks to build a big tower. It went up tall. "Push it!" said Milo. Wyatt tapped one block. Down came the tower, block by block. Wyatt put out his cup. "More water, please," he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Alice wanted to make soup for dinner. "I can help," she said. Dad said, "Yes, you can."

First, Alice put the carrots in the pot. Then she counted three potatoes. Dad dropped them in. Plop, plop, plop.

"Now we need an onion," said Dad. He picked up the knife. Alice stood back, way back.

Dad cut the onion into small squares. Then his eyes went drip, drip, drip. Big tears ran down his face.

"Dad, you are crying!" said Alice. "Are you sad about the soup?" She patted his arm.

Dad laughed. "Look at the onion, not me." Alice looked. The onion sat on the board, cut into squares. Dad blinked and blinked.

"It is the onion," he said. "Silly onion. It makes my eyes water."

Alice giggled. "Onion, you are a trickster!" she said.

They added the onion to the pot. Dad's eyes stopped dripping. Alice stirred with a big spoon, and the soup went round and round.

Then Mom came in. She sniffed the pot. "Mmm," she said. "Who cut the onion?"

Alice pointed at Dad. Dad made a funny crying face. Everyone laughed.

After dinner, Alice helped wash up. Then she yawned a big yawn. "Bath time," said Mom. Alice jumped in the tub. The water was warm. Her toes made little splashes.

"Dad," she called. "No onions in my bath!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Nathan stood on the ferry with his big brother Sam. The wind was cold. The water below was dark and wavy. "One suitcase, one backpack, one bear," Nathan counted. He hugged his bear tight.

Before the trip, Nathan had packed his blue swimsuit. "For swimming!" he had said. But Dad opened the suitcase and smiled. He held up Nathan's mittens and his warm red coat. "We are going to the snow," said Dad. "Snow needs mittens." Nathan put on the mittens. His hands felt cozy at once.

Now the ferry horn went honk, honk. Nathan looked out the window. White flakes began to fall on the black water. "Sam, look! Snow!" said Nathan. He waved his mittened hand at the sky, and one soft flake landed right on his brother's nose.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leon dumped out his big basket of picture cards. Cards went everywhere! He wanted to make a town with them. But the cards were all mixed up. He could not find what he needed.

Leon looked at a card with a cow. "You are an animal," he said. He made an animal pile. Cow, duck, and dog went there. Then he found a ball and a drum. "You are toys," he said. He made a toy pile. Then came apple, bread, and egg. "You are foods," he said. He made a food pile. Now the town had a farm, a toy shop, and a food store.

Leon lined the animals in a row. He followed them with his toy truck. The truck was carrying fresh apples to the store. Then a card fell from the pile. Leon picked it up. It was a little cat wearing a tiny hat! Leon laughed out loud. "You go with the animals," he said. "But you can keep the hat."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Lea sat on the city bus with Mama. She held a little card with her name on it. It was her first library card. On her lap was a big red book about a snowy day.

Lea opened the book. There was a cat in the snow. The cat had soft white fur. Lea put her finger on the page. She wanted to draw a hat on the cat. She took out her purple crayon. The crayon came closer and closer.

Then she saw small marks on the page corner. Other kids had held this book too. Lea looked at Mama. "This book is not mine," she said. Mama smiled and nodded.

Lea put the crayon away. She pulled a paper from her bag. On the paper, she drew a snowy hill. She drew a cat with a big purple hat. "There," said Lea. She closed the big red book very gently. The bus went beep, and Lea felt happy all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Rose wanted Grandpa to read her book about puppies. But Grandpa sat down and said, "One moment, Rose." He reached for his glasses. He put them on his nose.

Rose looked at the glasses with her eyes. "Why do you wear those?" she asked.

Grandpa opened the book. "Watch," he said. He read the first page slowly. Rose listened with her ears. She heard every word clearly.

Then Grandpa lifted the glasses off. He looked at the page. His eyes got wide. He turned the book toward Rose. The letters looked small and cloudy to him.

Rose touched the glasses gently with her fingers. They felt smooth and cool.

"I smell cookies," she said, sniffing with her nose. Grandpa laughed and put his glasses back on.

"Let's read, then eat," he said. "Mama made them sweet."

Rose tasted a warm cookie after the story. "Yum," she said, and Grandpa read the puppy book one more time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Felix went to the library with his mama. He wanted a book about dogs. He found a big red book with a black dog on the front. He showed it to a girl named Mia.

"That is a dog," said Mia. "Dogs are animals. My book has a cow. Cows are animals too."

Felix found a little blue book. A fish was on the cover. "Is a fish an animal?" he asked. "It has no legs."

"Let's look," said Mia. She put her book next to his. The fish book sat on the shelf under a sign. The sign said animals. The dog book was there. The cow book was there too.

"The fish is with them!" said Felix. He put his head close to the shelf. He tapped the fish book. "Fish, dog, cow. All animals."

The librarian smiled. "Would you like to take that one home?"

"Yes, please," said Felix. He hugged the blue book to his chest and walked to the desk, holding mama's hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Charlie got a new pet today. It was a little gray bunny. He carried the cage to the backyard. "Hello, bunny!" he said.

Charlie opened the cage door. But the bunny did not hop out. It hid in the corner. It stayed very still.

Charlie frowned. He wanted to pet the bunny. He reached in fast. The bunny moved back more.

"Mom, the bunny won't come!" said Charlie.

Mom came outside. "Let's sit on the grass," she said. "We can fill this bowl with bunny food and wait."

Charlie sat down on the warm grass. He put the food bowl near the cage. He sat very still, like a rock. It was hard to be so still.

Then Charlie heard a sound. Plop! The bunny hopped out! It sniffed the bowl. It nibbled the food. Charlie giggled softly.

"It feels safe now," Mom whispered.

Charlie smiled big. The bunny hopped one tiny hop closer.

"Hi, friend," said Charlie.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Hunter ran into the backyard. The sun felt warm on his face. Daddy was cooking at the grill. "Hot," said Daddy. "Stay back, please." Hunter stopped and watched. He could smell the food cooking. It smelled good.

Then Hunter saw his little slide. He wanted to slide down fast. He climbed up and sat down. He began to lie down on his tummy. His head went first. That felt wobbly. Hunter slid just a bit and stopped. He sat up and turned himself around. Now his feet went first. Down he went, whee, all the way to the grass.

Hunter ran to get his blocks. He stacked one block, then two, then three. The tower fell over into a messy pile. Hunter laughed. "Again!" he said. He put the first block down on the soft green grass.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Sienna sat on the big chair at the doctor's office. Her tummy felt stormy. "I will get a shot today," she said quietly. Mom held her hand. "I will stay right here," said Mom.

Nurse Amy came in with a small tray. Sienna saw the tiny needle. "Can I hold it?" she asked. "Only I touch the needle," said Nurse Amy kindly. "But you can hold my sticker sheet." Sienna took the sticker sheet. It had a flower on every sticker. She looked at the flowers while Nurse Amy gave the shot. It was done fast, like a little pinch. "All done!" said Nurse Amy. Sienna picked a pink flower sticker for her arm.

"Let's go get ice cream," said Mom. Sienna did not have to wait long. She got a cone with two scoops. She licked it and smiled. "My flower sticker matches my pink ice cream," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Leo ran to the play corner at school. His friend Mia was there. She put cushions on the floor.

"Watch out!" said Mia. "The floor is a river!"

Leo looked down. The floor did not look like a river. It was just brown and flat.

Mia hopped on a cushion. "Pretend it is a river," she said. "Pretend the cushions are rocks!"

Leo wanted to cross too. He wanted to get to the toy kitchen on the other side. He held his baby doll tight. He wanted to cook dinner for her.

Leo took a big jump. One rock! Then another jump. Two rocks! Then one more. Three rocks!

"You made it!" said Mia. "Now you are home."

Leo smiled. He sat at the toy kitchen. He turned the pretend knob. He stirred a pretend pot.

"Time to eat, baby," said Leo. He held the doll close. He patted her back, just like his mom did for his little sister.

Then Mia called, "The baby is cold!"

Leo looked around. He found a small blanket. He wrapped the doll up. "Nice and warm," he said.

"You are so kind to your baby," said Mia.

Just then a boy named Sam ran by. He stepped right on the floor river!

"Splash!" shouted Mia. "You fell in!"

Sam laughed and laughed. "I am a fish!" he said. He wiggled on the floor.

"Fish can come to dinner too," said Leo. He handed Sam a pretend cup.

Sam sat down. Mia sat down. The baby sat in Leo's lap.

"One soup, one cup, one warm baby," said Leo.

Mia clapped her hands. "Best dinner ever!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
James ran into writing club with his pet rabbit, Benny. "Today I write my name!" he said. His teacher, Miss Kim, smiled. She gave him a chunky pencil and a name card.

James held the pencil tight. He wrote J, then A, then S. Then he wrote a big M and another A. He looked at his paper. Something was wrong! Two letters had popped into the wrong spots. "Miss Kim, my name looks funny!" he said. She held up his name card. James looked. Then he looked again. The M came before the A, not after. He erased and fixed the letters, one by one.

He wrote his name once more, top to bottom. Same letters, same order, every time. "Benny, look!" he said. "My name is all full of letters, and they stay put!" He hugged the soft rabbit and wrote it again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Kayden ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. Warm bread and apple slices. Yum!

"Wash your hands first," said Mama.

Kayden stood at the sink. He pumped the soap. Bubbles grew on his hands. Mama helped him count. "One, two, three." They counted all the way to twenty. Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles!

Then the water went off. Kayden's hands were wet. He shook them. Drip, drip! Water fell on his shirt. Water fell on the floor. Little drops everywhere!

Where did the water go? Would it ever stop?

Then Kayden saw it. A blue towel hung on the hook. He reached up and took it. He rubbed one hand. Then the other. His hands went from wet to dry. All clean and dry!

He planted his dry hands on the bread. He held it tight. No slips, no drops. Kayden took a big bite.

"Mmm," he said. "Dry hands, yummy bread."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Wyatt dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped a carrot seed inside. He patted the dirt down with his hands. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every day Wyatt looked at his garden. One morning, tiny green leaves popped up. "Hello, leaves!" he said. But then he saw something else. Little green leaves were growing in the wrong spot too. Wyatt frowned. Were those his carrots? He reached down to pull one up.

Mom came outside with a spoon. "Wait, Wyatt," she said. "Let's look first." She knelt in the grass. "These leaves are in your seed line, straight in a row," she said. "Those other ones are not. Those are weeds. Weeds grow where we don't want them." Wyatt touched the weed leaf. "Not my carrot?" he asked. "Not your carrot," said Mom.

Wyatt pulled the weeds and put them in a bucket. His carrots got sun and water. Soon tall green tops stood in a straight row. Mom pulled one up. A fat orange carrot hung from the leaves. Wyatt took a bite and began to chew. "It grew!" he said. Mom smiled and held up the watering can. "More water for the others?"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Amira ran to the dress-up corner at school. She was so excited to wear the red cape. But Ben was there first. He had the cape on already. Amira felt angry. Her face got hot and her hands made fists. She wanted to grab the cape.

Then Amira heard a small sound. Drip. Drip. It was Leo, sitting close to the toy nest on the rug. Tears ran down his cheeks. Leo was sad. He was crying because his block tower had fallen down. Amira forgot all about the cape. She went to the rug and got her teddy bear. She put the teddy in Leo's hands.

Leo hugged the teddy tight. His tears stopped. Then he smiled a big smile. "Thank you, Amira," he said. Amira felt happy inside, warmer than any cape. Ben saw them and took off the red cape. "Your turn," he said. Amira put it on and twirled around the nest of soft toys. "Teddy helps sad friends," she told Leo. Leo nodded and clapped.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She had blocks of every shape. She picked a round one first. It rolled away! "Come back!" she laughed. The circle block would not stay still.

So she tried a square block. It sat nice and flat. She stacked another square on top. Then her friend Max came in. "Look!" he said. "That one is a new shape. It has a point at the top!" Lillian looked. She had turned one square sideways on the rug. "Is it a square?" she asked.

She turned the block back. Flat side down, it looked the same as before. She tilted it again. The point went up. "Silly block," she giggled. "You are still a square!" She stacked it back on the house. The snake slid in through the triangle roof and curled up on a rectangle block. "Perfect house," said Lillian.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Owen sat in the big waiting room chair. His feet did not touch the floor. He held his toy truck in both hands. Dad sat next to him and smiled.

"Owen," the nurse called. Owen stood up slow. He took one step, then one more. The nurse had a nice voice. She pointed to a little chair. Owen sat and held his truck tight.

"Will it hurt?" Owen asked.

"Just a quick pinch," said the nurse.

Owen felt the pinch. He blinked. Then it was done. Dad gave him a big hug. "All done," said Dad.

In the car, Owen rubbed his arm. "Ow," he said. "Why does my arm hurt?"

"That can happen after a shot," said Dad. "It will feel better soon."

Owen waited. He looked out the window. A red truck went by. He waved at it. Then he rubbed his arm again.

"Better now," said Owen. He held his truck up high. "Beep, beep!"
